title: Size and place a tenant's storage

blocks.text: The storage service places every new tenant: it gives the tenant a quota in bytes and picks the shard that holds each of the tenant's keys. Two reports came in after the last onboarding wave. A tenant with 4,000 users was given a negative quota and could store nothing. And one key of one tenant, out of millions, fails on every write with an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` from the shard router.
`TenantStorage.place` already puts the two answers together. Finish the two `TODO`s in `src/main/java/practice/TenantStorage.java`:

items: `quotaBytes(users, mbPerUser)`: the exact quota for any tenant the service accepts, up to tens of thousands of users with up to a hundred gigabytes each;
`shardFor(key)`: a shard from `0` to `shards - 1` for every key, the same one each time.

cases.says: a small tenant gets its exact quota, and each of its keys gets the same existing shard every time
a quota whose byte count is above Integer.MAX_VALUE is exact, although users times megabytes fits in an int
a quota is exact even when users times megabytes is already above Integer.MAX_VALUE
a key whose hashCode() is Integer.MIN_VALUE still gets a shard from 0 to shards - 1

origin.section: Integer Arithmetic Wraps Without an Error, Even When the Result Goes Into a long

concepts: int's range is asymmetric, so Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is negative and Math.abs(hash) % n can be a negative index; Math.floorMod takes the divisor's sign.
Integer arithmetic is done in the operands' type and wraps without an error, even when the result is assigned to a long; a long operand widens only the operations after it.
